citation: De Back, Tycho T., Angelica M. Tinga & Max M. Louwerse. (2021, published online 12 Dec; print issue 2023). Learning in immersed collaborative virtual environments: design and implementation. Interactive Learning Environments, 31(8), 5364–5382. https://doi.org/10.1080/10494820.2021.2006238
citationNote: Online-first 2021 / print-issue 2023 discrepancy (masthead reads '2023 ... 31:8, 5364-5382' but 'Published online: 12 Dec 2021' and the DOI registration are 2021). Kept id/slug/folder/year as manifest assigned them (2021, matching the plan's dating and filename); not blocking.
discipline: cognitive science / educational technology (VR learning-environment design; collaborative learning)
thesis: Existing VR-pedagogy frameworks (Dalgarno & Lee; Fowler; Mayer's cognitive theory of multimedia learning) are general and offer few concrete recommendations for immersive, especially collaborative, settings; this paper extends them into specific design recommendations across cognitive load, collaborative learning, platform affordances/limitations, and additional strategies, demonstrates them via a CAVE-based collaborative neuroanatomy environment shown to yield learning gains in two prior studies (n=40, n=158), and introduces a novel automated behavioral-performance-logging method for immersive settings.

sections.title: Introduction: the immersive-VLE design gap
sections.summary: Distinguishes non-immersive desktop VR from immersive VR (HMD/CAVE); notes existing frameworks (Dalgarno & Lee 2010; Fowler 2015; Mayer 2009/2014) offer general guidance but few concrete recommendations for immersive, collaborative settings; states the paper's aim.

sections.title: Theoretical framework: cognitive load
sections.summary: Reviews the three-load model (intrinsic/extraneous/germane) and Mayer's coherence, segmenting, and generative-processing principles as applied to IVR by Parong & Mayer (2018); adds pre-training as a further germane-load strategy; surveys supporting studies (Meyer et al. 2019; Lee & Wong 2014; Lin et al. 2019).

sections.title: Theoretical framework: collaborative learning & gamification
sections.summary: Positions IVR embodiment, avatar realism, and (non-)verbal communication as amplifiers of collaborative learning within Dalgarno & Lee's framework; reviews gamification as a further design lever with mixed empirical support.

sections.title: Recommendations for designing immersive VLEs
sections.summary: Translates the framework into five categories: optimizing cognitive load; fostering collaborative learning; leveraging platform-specific affordances; mitigating platform-specific limitations; additional strategies (gamification, modular design, automated performance analysis). Condensed in Table 1.

sections.title: Implementation: a collaborative CAVE-based neuroanatomy VLE
sections.summary: Details a two-year-developed CAVE environment (up to six learners) teaching neuroanatomy via exploration, reconstruction, and review phases; implements pre-training, segmenting, coherence (with one deliberate redundancy-principle violation), turn-based participation, and tracked-glasses perspective switching. Table 2, Figures 1-2.

sections.title: Empirical support and automated performance analysis
sections.summary: Reports learning gains over textbook instruction (Study 1, n=40, esp. low-spatial-ability learners) and replication at scale (Study 2, n=158, varying group size and timing of application). Introduces a dynamic automated-logging model tracking leader time, leaders observed, distance walked, head rotations, and face time, with a visual-replay feature, extending Chodos et al. (2014) and Fardinpour & Reiners (2014). Figures 3-4.

sections.title: Discussion and conclusion
sections.summary: Frames the recommendations as immersion-specific extensions of Dalgarno & Lee and Fowler; cautions IVR is 'no universal panacea'; flags the redundancy-principle violation as a context-dependent trade-off; gestures toward physiological/eye-tracking measures of cognitive load and AR extensions.

constructs.label: cognitive load (extraneous vs germane)
constructs.treatment: Three-load model plus coherence/segmenting/generative-processing/pre-training principles applied to the CAVE design; one deliberate redundancy-principle violation (simultaneous audio+text) justified post hoc by informal piloting, not a controlled test

constructs.label: presence (spatial/physical)
constructs.treatment: Invoked exactly once, generically, via Heeter (1992) and Steuer (1992) — 'the feeling of existing inside a virtual environment' — to justify pairing pre-training with a practice period; not social presence

constructs.label: embodiment / self-representation
constructs.treatment: Embodied 3D-mouse interaction, natural motions, tracked-glasses perspective switching; framed as amplifying collaborative learning within Dalgarno & Lee's learner-interaction feature group

constructs.label: engagement / flow
constructs.treatment: Approximated only via unlabeled behavioral proxies (leader time, distance walked, head rotations, face time) framed as correlates of 'behavioral engagement' (citing Lei et al. 2018); not a named or measured construct with an instrument

constructs.label: learning outcomes: retention & transfer
constructs.treatment: Study 1 (n=40) CAVE-vs-textbook gains, esp. low spatial ability; Study 2 (n=158) replication across group sizes and application timing

constructs.label: collaborative learning (source's own term; non-canonical, not equivalent to social presence/co-presence)
constructs.treatment: Operationalized procedurally — equal access, active/interdependent participation, visible interactions, turn-taking to limit social loafing — not measured via any scale or instrument

constructs.label: social presence / co-presence
constructs.treatment: NOT TREATED. Full-text check confirms the term never appears and none of the CMC-tradition Strand-F sources are cited. Retained as a row only to record this explicit negative finding, not because the source populates it.

constructNote: Confirms and extends the Phase-1 finding: 'social presence' is absent as a technical term throughout the full text; the paper's real construct content is cognitive load, embodiment, a bespoke 'collaborative learning' theme, and unlabeled behavioral-engagement proxies from its own logging model. Do not code any passage as treats-construct: social presence / co-presence.

conditions.label: IVR (HMD)
conditions.normalizedFrom: CAVE (Cave Automatic Virtual Environment) — the plan's §3 axis has no dedicated CAVE column; normalized here per the Phase-1 conditionsNote, with the mismatch flagged (CAVE differs from HMD in single- vs multi-user visibility and facial-expression transmission)
conditions.design: Study 1: CAVE-based collaborative neuroanatomy environment, 2-4 person groups, n=40 (participant pool, unfamiliar with subject). Study 2: same environment, undergraduate course, n=158; within-IVR manipulation of group size (1 / 2-4 / 5-6 persons) and timing of application (before/during/after course).
conditions.effectDirection: Study 1: CAVE > textbook, esp. low spatial ability. Study 2: gains present at all group sizes, inverse group-size gradient (smaller groups = larger gains); timing had no effect.

conditions.label: conventional instruction (control)
conditions.design: Textbook learning on neuroanatomy, Study 1 only (n=40, one arm of the two-arm comparison)

readings.claim: Existing VLE-design frameworks (Dalgarno & Lee 2010; Fowler 2015) are informative but not specific to immersive settings and contain few practical design recommendations for them.
Cognitive load in IVR should be managed via coherence, segmenting, pre-training, and generative processing; overload in one collaborator can affect interdependent others.
IVR amplifies collaborative learning via higher embodiment, richer (non-)verbal communication, and avatar realism relative to non-immersive VR.

A CAVE-based collaborative neuroanatomy environment built per these recommendations produced learning gains over textbook instruction (n=40), replicated at scale (n=158) across group sizes and application timings.

Deliberately violating Mayer's redundancy principle (simultaneous audio+text instruction) was net-beneficial in this specific CAVE context because of visibility occlusion, per informal piloting rather than a controlled test.

An automated performance-logging model dynamically adapting to different immersive technologies can extend prior fixed-category (Chodos et al. 2014) and unimplemented (Fardinpour & Reiners 2014) approaches, yielding both engagement metrics and a visual replay feature.
Immersive technologies are 'no universal panacea' for learning; they should be adopted only where a genuine match exists between intended learning outcomes and IVR-specific affordances.

tensions.axis: Strand-F placement as a 'CMC-to-VR social presence bridge' (cluster design assumption) vs. this paper's actual non-engagement with social presence theory
tensions.note: The strand was built to ground the cluster's previously-ungrounded 'social presence / co-presence' construct row; this paper looked, pre-full-text-check, like the natural VR-side bridge. Full-text verification shows it never uses the term and cites none of the CMC-tradition sources. The bridge is the cluster's own construction (P/anticipatory-application), not a claim this source makes. See manifest.json planCorrections entry for ped-sec-33.

tensions.axis: redundancy principle (Mayer) as a general design rule vs. this paper's own deliberate, context-justified violation of it
tensions.note: The CAVE case study presents instructions in both audio and text — a redundancy-principle violation — justified by informal piloting and CAVE-specific visibility occlusion, not by a controlled comparison; the paper frames this as a case-specific trade-off, not a general counter-recommendation.

tensions.axis: media-comparison design (Study 1: CAVE vs. textbook) vs. value-added/within-condition design (Study 2: group size and timing varied only within IVR)
tensions.note: Resonates with the cluster's debate axis 2 (media-comparison vs. methods-not-media/value-added paradigm, Mayer et al. 2022/ped-sec-07); this source uses both designs across its two studies without resolving the methodological debate.

bridgeNote: This paper does NOT itself bridge the CMC-tradition social-presence literature to VR — none of Short et al., Gunawardena & Zittle, Garrison/Anderson/Archer, Tu, Biocca/Burgoon/Harms, Kreijns/Kirschner/Jochems, Terry & Doolittle, or Richardson et al. are cited, and 'social presence' is never used. Its own bridging move runs from the general VR-pedagogy-framework literature (Dalgarno & Lee/ped-sec-04, Fowler/ped-sec-05, Parong & Mayer 2018/ped-sec-08, Merchant/ped-sec-16) into concrete collaborative/embodied design guidance. The CMC-to-VR bridge Strand F needs is this cluster's own construction, not something ped-sec-33 performs itself (see manifest.json planCorrections). On the VLE bridge: the CAVE environment's mandatory small-group collaboration and automated engagement metrics (face time, leader time, distance walked, head rotations) resonate with the VLE's own mandatory group-assignment design (per the VLE-proximity-voice correction bearing on vle-01's F7 finding) and exemplar co-watching quotes (vle-03); its behavioral-engagement logging also parallels vle-04's attention-span analysis approach, though no direct empirical overlap exists. Confirmed at Phase 2.
